title: Isaiah’s prophecy of the virgin
source_text: ἀλλ᾿ ὡς καὶ προφῆται προεῖπον, ἀπὸ παρθένου. κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν σημείου γεννώσης τὸν ἐπώνυμον πράγματος, δηλοῦντος ὅτι ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει αὐτοῦ μετ᾿ ἀνθρώπων ἔσται θεός. Καὶ οἰκεῖόν γε φαίνεταί μοι πρὸς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν παραθέσθαι τὴν τοῦ Ἡσαΐου προφητείαν, λέγουσαν ἐκ παρθένου τεχθήσεσθαι τὸν Ἐμμανουήλ· ἣν οὐκ ἐξέθετο, εἴτε μὴ ἐπιστάμενος ὁ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος εἴτ᾿ ἀναγνοὺς μὲν ἑκὼν δὲ σιωπήσας, ἵνα μὴ δοκοίη κατασκευάζειν ἄκων τὸν λόγον ἐναντιούμενον αὐτοῦ τῇ προαιρέσει. ἔχει δ᾿ οὕτως ἡ λέξις· „καὶ προσέθετο κύριος τῷ Ἄχαζ λέγων· αἴτησαι σεαυτῷ σημεῖον παρὰ κυρίου θεοῦ σου εἰς βάθος ἢ εἰς ὕψος. καὶ εἶπεν Ἄχαζ· οὐ μὴ αἰτήσω οὐδ᾿ οὐ μὴ πειράσω τὸν κύριον. (καὶ εἶπεν·) ἀκούσατε δὴ, οἶκος Δαυὶδ, μὴ μικρὸν ὑμῖν ἀγῶνα παρέχειν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ πῶς κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα; διὰ τοῦτο δώσει κύριος αὐτὸς ὑμῖν σημεῖον· ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται καὶ τέξεται υἱὸν, καὶ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ“, ὅπερ ἑρμηνεύεται „μεθ᾿ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός“. ὅτι δὲ κακουργῶν ὁ Κέλσος οὐκ ἐξέθετο τὴν προφητείαν, δῆλόν μοι γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ παραθέμενον αὐτὸν πολλὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγελίου, ὥσπερ τὸν ἀνατείλαντα ἀστέρα ἐπὶ τῇ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν παραδόξων, μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν τούτου ἐμνημονευκέναι. ἐὰν δὲ Ἰουδαῖος εὑρεσιλογῶν τὸ „ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος“ μὴ γεγράφθαι λέγῃ ἀλλ᾿ ἀντ᾿ αὐτοῦ „ἰδοὺ ἡ νεᾶνις“, φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ὅτι ἡ μὲν λέξις ἡ ἀαλμὰ, ἣν οἱ μὲν ἑβδομήκοντα μετειλήφασι πρὸς τὴν παρθένον ἄλλοι δ᾿ εἰς τὴν νεᾶνιν, κεῖται, ὥς φασι, καὶ ἐν τᾷ Δευτερονομίῳ ἐπὶ παρθένου, οὕτως ἔχουσα·„ἐὰν δὲ γένηται παῖς παρθένος μεμνηστευμένη ἀνδρὶ, καὶ εὑρὼν αὐτὴν ἄνθρωπος ἐν πόλει κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐξάξετε ἀμφοτέρους ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην τῆς πόλεως αὐτῶν, καὶ λιθοβοληθήσονται λίθοις, καὶ ἀποθανοῦνται· τὴν νεᾶνιν ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι οὐκ ἐβόησεν ἐν τῇ πόλει, καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπὶ λόγου, διότι ἐταπείνωσε τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον αὐτοῦ·“ καὶ ἑξῆς· „ἐὰν δὲ ἐν πεδίῳ εὕρῃ ἄνθρωπος τὴν παῖδα τὴν μεμνηστευμένην καὶ βιασάμενος αὐτὴν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κοιμηθῇ μετ᾿ αὐτῆς, ἀποκτενεῖτε τὸν ἄνθρωπον τὸν κοιμώμενον μετ᾿ αὐτῆς μόνον, καὶ τῇ νεάνιδι οὐ ποιήσετε οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔστι τῇ νεάνιδι ἁμάρτημα θανάτου.“
pass_a_gloss: But, as the prophets also foretold (προεῖπον), from a virgin (παρθένου) bearing, according to a promise of a sign (κατ᾿ ἐπαγγελίαν σημείου), the one named after a fact (τὸν ἐπώνυμον πράγματος), [a fact] showing that at his birth God will be with humans. And it seems to me proper (οἰκεῖον), with regard to the impersonation of the Jew (προσωποποιΐα), to set beside it (παραθέσθαι) the prophecy of Isaiah saying that Emmanuel will be born of a virgin; which Celsus did not set out (ἐξέθετο), either not knowing it, he who professes to know all things, or having read it but willingly kept silent (ἑκὼν σιωπήσας), lest he seem to construct (κατασκευάζειν) unwillingly the argument opposed to his purpose (προαίρεσις). The wording (λέξις) is thus: [Isaiah 7:10-14 LXX: Lord spoke further to Ahaz; ask a sign from the Lord your God into depth or height; Ahaz: I will not ask nor tempt (πειράσω) the Lord; hear, house of David, is it a small thing for you to provide a contest/trouble (ἀγῶνα παρέχειν) to men, and how do you provide a contest to the Lord? therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold the virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you (sg.) will call his name Emmanuel], which is interpreted (ἑρμηνεύεται) 'with us God'. That Celsus acting maliciously (κακουργῶν) did not set out the prophecy becomes clear to me from his having cited many things from the Gospel according to Matthew, like the star that rose (ἀνατείλαντα ἀστέρα) at the birth of Jesus and others of the marvels, and not to have mentioned this at all (μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν). And if a Jew, quibbling (εὑρεσιλογῶν), says 'behold the virgin' is not written but instead 'behold the young woman' (νεᾶνις), we shall say to him that the word aalma, which the Seventy translated (μετειλήφασι) as 'the virgin' and others as 'the young woman', lies (κεῖται), as they say, also in Deuteronomy of a virgin, thus: [Deut 22:23-24 LXX: if there be a girl virgin (παῖς παρθένος) betrothed (μεμνηστευμένη) to a man and a man finding her in the city lies with her, you shall bring both out to the gate of their city, and they shall be stoned with stones and die: the young woman (νεᾶνιν) because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he humbled (ἐταπείνωσε) the wife of his neighbour]; and next: [Deut 22:25-26 LXX: if in the field a man finds the betrothed girl and forcing (βιασάμενος) her lies with her, you shall kill only the man lying with her, and to the young woman you shall do nothing; there is not for the young woman a sin of death (ἁμάρτημα θανάτου)].
pass_b_english: Rather, as the prophets also foretold, it had to come from a virgin who, according to the promise of a sign, would give birth to one named after a fact, a fact which showed that at his birth God would be with human beings (Isaiah 7:14).

And it seems to me fitting, in answer to the Jew whom Celsus impersonates, to set out the prophecy of Isaiah, which says that Emmanuel would be born of a virgin. Celsus did not quote it. Either he did not know it, for all that he professes to know everything, or he had read it and chose to keep silent, so as not to seem to be unwittingly building up an argument that tells against his own purpose. The passage reads as follows: “And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height. And Ahaz said: I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test. And he said: Hear then, house of David: is it a small thing for you to make trouble for men? And how is it that you make trouble for the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:10–14), which is interpreted “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).

That Celsus left the prophecy out in bad faith is clear to me from this: he cites a great deal from the Gospel according to Matthew, such as the star that rose at the birth of Jesus (Matthew 2:2) and other wonders, yet he makes no mention of this at all. But if a Jew quibbles and says that the text does not read “Behold, the virgin” but instead “Behold, the young woman,” we shall reply to him that the word aalma, which the Seventy rendered “the virgin” and others “the young woman,” also occurs, so they say, in Deuteronomy of a virgin, as follows: “If there is a girl, a virgin, betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of their city, and they shall be stoned with stones and shall die: the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he dishonoured his neighbour’s wife” (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). And next: “But if a man finds the betrothed girl in the field, and the man forces her and lies with her, you shall put to death only the man who lay with her, and to the young woman you shall do nothing; the young woman has committed no sin deserving death” (Deuteronomy 22:25–26).

choices.choice: The opening clause completes the sentence of 1.33 (the body had to come into being 'not of Panthera... but, as the prophets foretold, of a virgin'). Isaiah 7:10-14 is quoted from the Septuagint; 'make trouble' renders ἀγῶνα παρέχειν (LXX for Hebrew 'weary'). 'Which is interpreted God with us' follows the gloss in Matthew 1:23 rather than Isaiah itself. 'The star that rose' alludes to Matthew 2:2 (also 2:9). Deuteronomy 22:23-26 is quoted from the Septuagint. Origen's claim, introduced with 'so they say' (ὥς φασι), that the Hebrew word of Isaiah 7:14 ('almah) stands in Deuteronomy 22 is not borne out by the Masoretic text, which has na'arah betulah there; the LXX of that passage uses νεᾶνις, which may be the source of the report. Translated as written, without correction. The staged text has ἐν τᾷ Δευτερονομίῳ; read τῷ. 'aalma' is Origen's transliteration (ἀαλμά), kept as written. 'The Seventy' are the Septuagint translators. 'The Jew whom Celsus impersonates' renders τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν (Celsus speaking in the person of a Jew).
opening: 'it was born of a virgin who ... would bear' (tense clash) -> 'it had to come from a virgin who ... would give birth', continuing ἔδει γενέσθαι σῶμα of 1.33
δηλοῦντος (a fact showing that): 'whose name matched a fact: the fact that' -> 'named after a fact, a fact which showed that'
προσωποποιΐαν: 'the speech Celsus puts in the mouth of his Jew' -> 'the Jew whom Celsus impersonates'
ἄκων τὸν λόγον: 'build, against his will, the argument that runs counter' -> 'be unwittingly building up an argument that tells against his own purpose'
ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται: 'conceive in the womb' -> 'conceive in her womb'
